title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
text:
Show R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define our consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Count only one medal per unique event and country so team sports are not overcounted
medals_unique <- olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal)) |> # Keep only medal-winning entries
  distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) # Deduplicate team medals

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: Methodology: Counting Medals Fairly & Defining Europe
text:
Methodology: Counting Medals Fairly & Defining Europe

Two important methodological choices from Milestone 3 make our comparisons between the United States and Europe accurate and fair:

Counting unique event medals instead of athlete rows: In the raw dataset, every player on a winning basketball, soccer, or rowing team gets their own row. If we simply counted rows, a single basketball gold medal would count as 12 medals! To avoid overcounting team sports, I use distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) so that each country receives one medal per event.
Consistent European Selection (12 Countries): Throughout all charts, I use a clearly defined set of 12 European Olympic countries: Spain (ESP), Great Britain (GBR), France (FRA), Germany (GER), Italy (ITA), Sweden (SWE), Norway (NOR), Netherlands (NED), Hungary (HUN), Finland (FIN), Switzerland (SUI), and Poland (POL).


Why Group vs. Individual Comparisons Matter: Comparing the United States (2,823 medals) against 12 European countries combined (6,849 medals) is very different from comparing individual countries. In the Olympics, each European nation sends its own full delegation of athletes and teams, so combining 12 countries naturally produces a larger group total. However, when we compare individual countries one-on-one, the United States (2,823 medals) has won nearly three times as many medals as the highest-ranking European country in our group, Germany (1,004), followed by Great Britain (919) and France (879).

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: 1. USA vs. Europe: Olympic Medals Over Time (1896–2016)
text:
1. USA vs. Europe: Olympic Medals Over Time (1896–2016)

This interactive chart tracks total unique event medals won in each Olympic year from 1896 to 2016 (combining Summer and Winter Games held in the same year). You can hover over any point to see the exact year and medal total.
Notice how the 12 European countries combined usually win more medals as a group, while the United States alone reaches massive peaks (such as 1904 in St. Louis and 1984 in Los Angeles) and competes closely with an entire continent’s worth of teams.


Show R Code
# Count unique event medals by Year for the USA vs. the 12 selected European countries
medals_by_year <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Year, Group, name = "Medals")

# Create the ggplot2 time-series line chart
p1 <- ggplot(medals_by_year, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, color = Group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries Combined)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1896, 2016, by = 16)) +
  labs(
    title = "USA vs. Selected European Countries: Unique Event Medals Over Time",
    subtitle = "Combined Summer & Winter Olympic medals per Olympic year (1896–2016)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

# Convert to an interactive Plotly chart
ggplotly(p1, tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: 2. Country-by-Country Breakdown: USA vs. Each of the 12 European Nations
text:
2. Country-by-Country Breakdown: USA vs. Each of the 12 European Nations

To see how the United States compares against each of the 12 European countries individually, the interactive stacked bar chart below breaks down total unique event medals (Gold, Silver, and Bronze) won by each country from 1896 to 2016.
Viewed nation by nation, the United States (2,823 total medals: 1,131 Gold, 901 Silver, 791 Bronze) stands far ahead of every individual European country, followed by Germany (1,004), Great Britain (919), France (879), Italy (722), and Sweden (657).


Show R Code
# Map NOC codes to readable country labels
country_labels <- c(
  "USA" = "United States (USA)",
  "GER" = "Germany (GER)",
  "GBR" = "Great Britain (GBR)",
  "FRA" = "France (FRA)",
  "ITA" = "Italy (ITA)",
  "SWE" = "Sweden (SWE)",
  "HUN" = "Hungary (HUN)",
  "NOR" = "Norway (NOR)",
  "FIN" = "Finland (FIN)",
  "NED" = "Netherlands (NED)",
  "SUI" = "Switzerland (SUI)",
  "POL" = "Poland (POL)",
  "ESP" = "Spain (ESP)"
)

country_medals <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  mutate(
    Country = country_labels[NOC],
    Medal = factor(Medal, levels = c("Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))
  ) |>
  count(Country, Medal, name = "Medals") |>
  mutate(Country = fct_reorder(Country, Medals, .fun = sum))

p_countries <- ggplot(country_medals, aes(x = Country, y = Medals, fill = Medal)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gold" = "#fbbf24",
      "Silver" = "#cbd5e1",
      "Bronze" = "#ec4899"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Country Comparison: USA vs. 12 European Nations (1896–2016)",
    subtitle = "Total unique event medals broken down by Gold, Silver, and Bronze",
    x = "Country (NOC)",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Medal Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_countries, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.25, y = 1.12)
  )

title: USA vs. Europe: 120 Years of Olympic Competition
section: 3. Focus on Spain: Olympic Medal History (1900–2016)
text:
3. Focus on Spain: Olympic Medal History (1900–2016)

Because I am from Spain (ESP), I wanted to take a closer look at how Spain’s Olympic performance has evolved over time. Through 2016, Spain has won 150 unique event medals (45 Gold, 63 Silver, and 42 Bronze), with its top sports being Sailing (19 medals), Canoeing (16), Cycling (15), Athletics (14), and Tennis (12).
As the chart below clearly shows, 1992 was the turning point in Spanish Olympic history. When Barcelona hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics, Spain invested heavily in athlete training and won 23 total medals in 1992 (22 in Summer—including 13 Golds—and 1 Bronze in Winter). Since 1992, Spain has remained a strong Olympic contender at every Summer Games through 2016.


Show R Code
# Filter unique medals for Spain (ESP) and order Medal factor levels
spain_medals <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC == "ESP") |>
  mutate(Medal = factor(Medal, levels = c("Gold", "Silver", "Bronze"))) |>
  count(Year, Medal, name = "Medals")

# Create a stacked bar chart of Spain's medals over time
p3 <- ggplot(spain_medals, aes(x = Year, y = Medals, fill = Medal)) +
  geom_col(width = 2.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gold" = "#fbbf24",   # Gold accent
      "Silver" = "#cbd5e1", # Crisp silver
      "Bronze" = "#ec4899"  # Vibrant pink accent for Bronze
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2016, by = 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Spain's Olympic Medal History by Medal Type (1900–2016)",
    subtitle = "Notice the dramatic breakthrough at the 1992 Barcelona Games (23 total medals)",
    x = "Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won by Spain",
    fill = "Medal Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p3, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.25, y = 1.12)
  )

title: About This Project
text:
Author: Emma Acedo Lapieza
Project: Milestone 6 — Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics? (1896–2016)
GitHub Repository: https://github.com/emmaacedoo/beyond-the-medals
Published Website: https://emmaacedoo.github.io/beyond-the-medals/

I created this project because I love sports and wanted to explore 120 years of Olympic history through data science in R and Quarto. Coming from Spain (ESP), I was especially curious to see how European nations compare against the United States—both individually and as a combined group—how national GDP relates to Olympic medal counts, and how Spain’s Olympic medal performance changed during and after the 1992 Barcelona Olympics.

title: About This Project
text:
Project Overview & Key Findings

Looking at 120 years of Olympic data from 1896 to 2016, our multi-page exploration reveals five core takeaways:

Individual Athlete Physical Profiles (14,553 Plotted Observations on the Homepage):

On the Home page, we plot 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations directly (4,595 from the United States and 9,958 from the 12 selected European countries) with recorded Age and Height.
Each point represents a single athlete-event observation, showing that U.S. Olympic medalists are on average slightly younger (24.6 years vs. 26.6 years) and taller (180.0 cm vs. 178.0 cm) than their European counterparts.

Group vs. Single-Country Medal Dominance (USA vs. Europe):

As a group of 12 countries, our selected European nations (ESP, GBR, FRA, GER, ITA, SWE, NOR, NED, HUN, FIN, SUI, POL) have won more combined unique event medals (6,849) than the United States (2,823), because 12 separate nations can enter many more athletes and teams across every event.
As a single country, the United States (2,823 medals) is by far the most dominant individual nation in Olympic history, winning nearly triple the medals of the highest-ranking European country in our group, Germany (1,004), followed by Great Britain (919) and France (879).

Sport Specialization (Sports):

Even against all 12 European countries combined, the United States leads in Swimming (550 vs. 411) and is virtually tied in Athletics (816 vs. 822), while the 12 European nations hold large collective advantages in Fencing (424 vs. 32), Cycling (423 vs. 57), Canoeing (329 vs. 16), and Rowing (314 vs. 89).

Does Money Buy Olympic Success? (Money & Medals):

Combining World Bank GDP (NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, 1960–2016) with verified Olympic country codes shows a strong positive correlation between log-GDP and log-medals (\(r = 0.72\) in Rio 2016), while also demonstrating why GDP is not direct sports funding and why correlation does not prove causation.

Spain’s 1992 Barcelona Turning Point (Barcelona 1992):

Through 2016, Spain (ESP) has won 150 unique event medals (45 Gold, 63 Silver, and 42 Bronze), led by Sailing (19), Canoeing (16), Cycling (15), Athletics (14), and Tennis (12). Spain’s Summer Olympic results jumped from an average of 1.6 medals per Games before 1992 (26 Summer medals across 16 Games) to 22 Summer medals (13 Gold) at the 1992 Barcelona Summer Olympics, and remained elevated at 16.7 medals per Games from 1996 to 2016.

title: About This Project
text:
Dataset Attribution & Reproducibility


Dataset 1 (Olympic Athletes & Results): 120 Years of Olympic History: Athletes and Results

Author / Curator: rgriffin (heesoo37) on Kaggle (originally scraped from www.sports-reference.com in May 2018)
Scope & Size: 271,116 rows and 15 columns covering all Summer and Winter Olympic Games from Athens 1896 to Rio 2016 (data/athlete_events.csv and data/noc_regions.csv).

Dataset 2 (National GDP): World Bank World Development Indicators — GDP (current US$, NY.GDP.MKTP.CD)

Scope & Size: Annual national GDP in current US dollars (1960–2016), stored locally in data/world_bank_gdp.csv and automatically retrievable via the official World Bank REST API (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD).

Key Variables Used:

ID, Name, Sex, Age, Height (cm), Weight (kg)
Team, NOC (3-letter National Olympic Committee code), iso3c (ISO-3166 alpha-3 code)
Games, Year, Season, City
Sport, Event, Medal (Gold, Silver, Bronze, or NA), gdp_usd (World Bank GDP in current US$)



Reproducibility in This Repository
All three CSV files (data/athlete_events.csv, data/noc_regions.csv, and data/world_bank_gdp.csv) are included directly in the data/ folder of this repository so that cloning the repository and running quarto render reproduces the entire website immediately without external dependencies.
If you ever need to download a fresh copy from Kaggle using the Kaggle CLI:
mkdir -p data
kaggle datasets download -d heesoo37/120-years-of-olympic-history-athletes-and-results -p data --unzip

title: Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
text:
Show R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
# If the local CSV is missing, inform how to place or download it from Kaggle
if (!file.exists("data/athlete_events.csv")) {
  stop("Dataset file 'data/athlete_events.csv' not found. Please place the Kaggle '120 Years of Olympic History' CSV in the data/ folder.")
}

olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define a consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Prepare individual medal-winning athlete observations with non-missing Age and Height
# Each row represents a single individual athlete-event observation (n = 14,553)
set.seed(2026)
medalists_individual <- olympics |>
  filter(
    NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs),
    !is.na(Medal),
    !is.na(Age),
    !is.na(Height)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    ),
    # Small deterministic jitter (+/- 0.35) so athletes with identical integer Age & Height don't stack
    Age_Plot = Age + runif(n(), -0.35, 0.35),
    Height_Plot = Height + runif(n(), -0.35, 0.35),
    Hover_Info = paste0(
      "<b>", Name, "</b> (", Team, " · ", NOC, ")<br>",
      "Region: ", Region, "<br>",
      "Age: <b>", Age, " yrs</b> | Height: <b>", Height, " cm</b>",
      if_else(!is.na(Weight), paste0(" | Weight: ", Weight, " kg"), ""), "<br>",
      "Games: ", Games, " (", City, ")<br>",
      "Sport: ", Sport, "<br>",
      "Event: ", Event, "<br>",
      "Medal: <b>", Medal, "</b>"
    )
  )

title: Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
Europe vs. America: Who Dominates the Olympics?
section: Athlete Physical Profiles: Age vs. Height (14,553 Individual Observations)
text:
Athlete Physical Profiles: Age vs. Height (14,553 Individual Observations)

Rather than looking only at aggregated totals, the interactive scatterplot below plots 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations directly from 1896 to 2016—every single medalist entry with recorded Age and Height from the United States (4,595 individual observations) and our 12 selected European countries (9,958 individual observations: ESP, GBR, FRA, GER, ITA, SWE, NOR, NED, HUN, FIN, SUI, and POL).

Each point is one individual athlete-event observation (not an average or aggregated group).
Hover over any point to inspect that athlete’s name, country (NOC), exact age (years), exact height (cm), weight (kg), Olympic Games, sport, event, and medal won (Gold, Silver, or Bronze).
Click items in the legend to toggle between the United States (#fbbf24 gold) and Selected Europe (#a855f7 purple), or drag to zoom into specific age and height ranges.



Show R Code
# Build the scatterplot of 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations
p_scatter <- ggplot(
  medalists_individual,
  aes(x = Age_Plot, y = Height_Plot, color = Region)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = Hover_Info),
    alpha = 0.48,
    size = 1.45
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = Age, y = Height, color = Region),
    method = "gam",
    formula = y ~ s(x, bs = "cs"),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.25
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(15, 65, by = 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(140, 225, by = 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "Age vs. Height of Olympic Medalists: USA vs. Europe (14,553 Individual Observations)",
    subtitle = "Each point is an individual medalist observation (4,595 USA · 9,958 Selected Europe, 1896–2016)",
    x = "Athlete Age at the Olympics (Years)",
    y = "Athlete Height (cm)",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

# Render with WebGL so all 14,553 individual points remain fast and responsive
ggplotly(p_scatter, tooltip = "text") |>
  toWebGL() |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.11)
  )







What Do These 14,553 Individual Observations Reveal?

Exact Observation Count: A total of 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations with complete Age and Height records are plotted directly above (4,595 from the United States and 9,958 from the 12 selected European countries).
American Medalists Are Slightly Younger and Taller on Average: Across all plotted observations, U.S. medalists have a younger average age (24.6 years, median 24) and taller average height (180.0 cm, median 180 cm) compared to European medalists (26.6 years, median 26; 178.0 cm, median 178 cm). This reflects strong U.S. collegiate (NCAA) participation in sports like Swimming, Athletics, and Basketball.
Age & Height Span Across Sports: The cloud of points spans from young teenage medalists in Gymnastics, Diving, and Swimming (ages 13–17, often 140–165 cm) to tall medalists above 205 cm in Basketball and Rowing, as well as veteran medalists competing into their 40s, 50s, and 60s in Equestrianism, Sailing, Shooting, and Fencing.

title: Does Money Buy Olympic Success?
text:
Show R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(countrycode)
library(jsonlite)

# 1. Load the Olympic dataset (1896–2016)
olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Load real World Bank GDP data (indicator NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, current US$, 1960–2016)
# Fetches directly from the World Bank REST API if the local CSV cache is not present
wb_cache_path <- "data/world_bank_gdp.csv"
if (!file.exists(wb_cache_path)) {
  wb_url <- "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.CD?date=1960:2016&format=json&per_page=20000"
  wb_raw <- fromJSON(wb_url)
  wb_gdp <- as_tibble(wb_raw[[2]]) |>
    transmute(
      iso3c = countryiso3code,
      country_wb = country$value,
      Year = as.integer(date),
      gdp_usd = as.numeric(value)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(iso3c), nchar(iso3c) == 3, !is.na(gdp_usd)) |>
    arrange(iso3c, Year)
  write_csv(wb_gdp, wb_cache_path)
} else {
  wb_gdp <- read_csv(wb_cache_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
}

# Define our consistent 12 selected European countries from the rest of the website
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", "GBR", "FRA", "GER", "ITA", "SWE",
  "NOR", "NED", "HUN", "FIN", "SUI", "POL"
)

# Historical, dissolved, or multi-state Olympic NOCs that cannot be mapped 1-to-1
# to a single modern sovereign country's World Bank GDP series
excluded_historical_nocs <- c(
  "URS", # Soviet Union
  "GDR", # East Germany
  "FRG", # West Germany
  "EUN", # Unified Team (1992 post-Soviet republics)
  "TCH", # Czechoslovakia
  "YUG", # Yugoslavia
  "SCG", # Serbia and Montenegro
  "UAR", # United Arab Republic
  "WIF", # West Indies Federation
  "AHO", # Netherlands Antilles
  "IOA", # Individual Olympic Athletes
  "ROT", # Refugee Olympic Team
  "EUA", # United Team of Germany
  "RHO"  # Rhodesia
)

# Build a verified NOC-to-ISO3 lookup table for Olympic years >= 1960
noc_iso_lookup <- olympics |>
  filter(Year >= 1960) |>
  distinct(NOC) |>
  mutate(
    iso3c = case_when(
      NOC %in% excluded_historical_nocs ~ NA_character_,
      NOC == "LIB" ~ "LBN", # Lebanon competed under IOC code LIB through 2016
      NOC == "SIN" ~ "SGP", # Singapore competed under IOC code SIN through 2016
      NOC == "KOS" ~ "XKX", # Kosovo uses XKX in World Bank data
      TRUE ~ countrycode(NOC, origin = "ioc", destination = "iso3c", warn = FALSE)
    )
  )

# Deduplicate team events so each country receives 1 medal per unique event
# Restrict to 1960–2016 (years when World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD data is available)
medals_unique_1960 <- olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal), Year >= 1960) |>
  distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal)

# Count unique event medals by NOC and Summer Olympic year (1960–2016)
# Note: In 1960 and 1964, GER represented the combined United Team of Germany (East + West),
# so we exclude GER in 1960 and 1964 to avoid mismatching a combined team to single-state GDP.
summer_medals_by_noc <- medals_unique_1960 |>
  filter(
    Season == "Summer",
    !(NOC == "GER" & Year %in% c(1960, 1964))
  ) |>
  group_by(Year, Games, NOC) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Medals = n(),
    Gold = sum(Medal == "Gold"),
    Silver = sum(Medal == "Silver"),
    Bronze = sum(Medal == "Bronze"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(noc_iso_lookup, by = "NOC") |>
  filter(!is.na(iso3c)) |>
  inner_join(wb_gdp, by = c("iso3c", "Year")) |>
  mutate(
    GDP_Billions = gdp_usd / 1e9,
    Medals_Per_100B_GDP = round(Total_Medals / (gdp_usd / 1e11), 2),
    Group = case_when(
      NOC == "USA" ~ "United States (USA)",
      NOC == "ESP" ~ "Spain (ESP)",
      NOC %in% euro_nocs ~ "Selected Europe (Other 11 Countries)",
      TRUE ~ "Rest of World"
    ),
    Group = factor(
      Group,
      levels = c(
        "United States (USA)",
        "Spain (ESP)",
        "Selected Europe (Other 11 Countries)",
        "Rest of World"
      )
    ),
    Hover_Text = paste0(
      "<b>", country_wb, "</b> (NOC: ", NOC, " · ISO3: ", iso3c, ")<br>",
      "Olympic Games: <b>", Games, "</b><br>",
      "Region Group: ", Group, "<br>",
      "World Bank GDP: <b>$", formatC(GDP_Billions, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ","), " Billion</b><br>",
      "Unique Event Medals: <b>", Total_Medals, "</b> (Gold: ", Gold, " · Silver: ", Silver, " · Bronze: ", Bronze, ")<br>",
      "Medals per $100B GDP: <b>", Medals_Per_100B_GDP, "</b>"
    )
  )

title: Does Money Buy Olympic Success?
section: 1. Interactive Exploration: GDP vs. Unique Olympic Event Medals (1960–2016)
text:
1. Interactive Exploration: GDP vs. Unique Olympic Event Medals (1960–2016)

Does the size of a country’s economy predict how many Olympic medals it wins? To investigate this question, I combined the Olympic dataset (data/athlete_events.csv) with real World Bank Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data in current US dollars (indicator NY.GDP.MKTP.CD). Because World Bank GDP records begin in 1960, this exploration covers the 15 Summer Olympic Games from Rome 1960 to Rio 2016.
Use the Olympic Year dropdown menu at the top-left of the chart below (or click items in the legend) to explore how the relationship between national GDP and unique Olympic event medals has evolved from 1960 to 2016:

X-Axis (Log Scale): National GDP in current US dollars ($100M, $1B, $10B, $100B, $1T, $10T · NY.GDP.MKTP.CD).
Y-Axis: Unique Summer Olympic event medals won (distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal) so team sports count as one medal per event).
Hover over any country to inspect its World Bank country name, Olympic NOC, ISO3 code, exact GDP ($ Billions), total unique event medals (Gold, Silver, Bronze), and medals per $100 Billion of GDP.



Show R Code
# Prepare year-by-year traces so readers can switch cleanly across all 15 Summer Olympic years (1960–2016)
# or view 2016 immediately on load with full interactive hover details
summer_years <- sort(unique(summer_medals_by_noc$Year))
default_year <- 2016

group_colors <- c(
  "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24",
  "Spain (ESP)" = "#ec4899",
  "Selected Europe (Other 11 Countries)" = "#a855f7",
  "Rest of World" = "#38bdf8"
)

fig <- plot_ly()

# Add 4 group traces per Olympic year (15 years * 4 groups = 60 traces)
for (yr in summer_years) {
  yr_data <- summer_medals_by_noc |> filter(Year == yr)
  is_vis <- (yr == default_year)
  
  for (grp in names(group_colors)) {
    grp_data <- yr_data |> filter(Group == grp)
    fig <- fig |>
      add_trace(
        data = grp_data,
        x = ~GDP_Billions,
        y = ~Total_Medals,
        type = "scatter",
        mode = "markers",
        name = grp,
        legendgroup = grp,
        showlegend = is_vis,
        visible = is_vis,
        text = ~Hover_Text,
        hoverinfo = "text",
        marker = list(
          size = ~pmax(9, pmin(26, sqrt(Total_Medals) * 2.6)),
          color = group_colors[[grp]],
          opacity = 0.88,
          line = list(color = "#0b1021", width = 1.2)
        )
      )
  }
}

# Build interactive dropdown items for each Summer Olympic year from 1960 to 2016
year_dropdown_buttons <- lapply(seq_along(summer_years), \(i) {
  yr <- summer_years[i]
  vis_vec <- rep(FALSE, length(summer_years) * 4)
  idx_start <- (i - 1) * 4 + 1
  vis_vec[idx_start:(idx_start + 3)] <- TRUE
  
  yr_rows <- summer_medals_by_noc |> filter(Year == yr)
  r_val <- round(cor(log10(yr_rows$GDP_Billions), log10(yr_rows$Total_Medals)), 2)
  
  list(
    method = "update",
    args = list(
      list(visible = vis_vec, showlegend = vis_vec),
      list(
        title = list(
          text = paste0(
            "World Bank GDP vs. Unique Summer Olympic Medals in ", yr,
            " (Log-Log r = ", r_val, " · ", nrow(yr_rows), " Matched Countries)"
          ),
          x = 0.01,
          y = 0.97,
          xanchor = "left",
          font = list(color = "#f8fafc", size = 15)
        )
      )
    ),
    label = paste0("Summer Olympics: ", yr)
  )
})

r_2016 <- round(
  cor(
    log10(summer_medals_by_noc$GDP_Billions[summer_medals_by_noc$Year == 2016]),
    log10(summer_medals_by_noc$Total_Medals[summer_medals_by_noc$Year == 2016])
  ),
  2
)
n_2016 <- sum(summer_medals_by_noc$Year == 2016)

fig |>
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "World Bank GDP vs. Unique Summer Olympic Medals in 2016 (Log-Log r = ",

      type = "log",
      tickmode = "array",

      tickfont = list(color = "#cbd5e1")
    ),

title: Does Money Buy Olympic Success?
section: 2. Why Country Matching & Limitations Matter: Correlation \(\neq\) Causation
text:
2. Why Country Matching & Limitations Matter: Correlation \(\neq\) Causation

Linking international economic statistics to Olympic records requires careful country matching. Because International Olympic Committee (NOC) codes often differ from the World Bank’s ISO-3166 alpha-3 (iso3c) codes, I mapped each modern NOC to its verified iso3c code and excluded dissolved or multi-state historical teams that cannot be matched to a single country’s modern World Bank GDP series.
Crucially, GDP is not direct sports investment. World Bank indicator NY.GDP.MKTP.CD measures total national economic output across all goods and services—not athletic budgets, coaching systems, or community facilities. For instance, in Rio 2016, Great Britain (GBR, GDP $2.7T, 67 medals) and India (IND, GDP $2.3T, 2 medals) had comparable total GDP, yet very different Olympic outcomes. Neither total GDP nor elite sports funding alone explains this gap; Olympic medal totals reflect a complex mix of historical sporting traditions, grass-roots participation, per-capita income and public infrastructure, and which sports are included on the Olympic program (for example, cricket is India’s most popular sport but was not contested in 1960–2016).
Finally, correlation does not prove causation. Although log-transformed GDP and log-transformed medal totals correlate strongly in 2016 (\(r = 0.72\) across 84 matched medal-winning countries), a larger economy does not automatically cause Olympic victories. Total GDP is heavily confounded with population size, living standards, leisure time, and sports infrastructure, while countries such as Jamaica (JAM, 11 medals with $14.1B GDP), Kenya (KEN, 13 medals with $74.8B GDP), and Cuba (CUB, 11 medals with $91.4B GDP) regularly win far more medals than their GDP alone would predict through deep cultural specialization.


Show Detailed NOC-to-ISO3 Country Matching & Excluded Historical Delegations



Verified Code Translations: Olympic NOC codes such as GER (Germany), ESP (Spain), NED (Netherlands), SUI (Switzerland), GRE (Greece), POR (Portugal), DEN (Denmark), CRO (Croatia), SLO (Slovenia), RSA (South Africa), LIB (Lebanon), SIN (Singapore), and KOS (Kosovo) are mapped explicitly to their ISO-3166 alpha-3 equivalents (DEU, ESP, NLD, CHE, GRC, PRT, DNK, HRV, SVN, ZAF, LBN, SGP, and XKX) using countrycode plus verified manual rules for pre-2016 IOC codes.
Excluded Historical & Multi-State Delegations: To prevent silent mismatches, the following historical or non-sovereign Olympic delegations are excluded rather than forced onto modern single-country GDP series: Soviet Union (URS), East Germany (GDR), West Germany (FRG), Unified Team (EUN, 1992), Czechoslovakia (TCH), Yugoslavia (YUG), Serbia and Montenegro (SCG), United Arab Republic (UAR), West Indies Federation (WIF), Netherlands Antilles (AHO), Individual Olympic Athletes (IOA), Refugee Olympic Team (ROT), and the 1960–1964 United Team of Germany (GER), when East and West Germany competed together as a single combined delegation.

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

# Load the Kaggle Olympic dataset (271,116 rows and 15 columns)
olympics <- read_csv("data/athlete_events.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Define our consistent group of 12 major European Olympic countries (including Spain)
euro_nocs <- c(
  "ESP", # Spain
  "GBR", # Great Britain
  "FRA", # France
  "GER", # Germany
  "ITA", # Italy
  "SWE", # Sweden
  "NOR", # Norway
  "NED", # Netherlands
  "HUN", # Hungary
  "FIN", # Finland
  "SUI", # Switzerland
  "POL"  # Poland
)

# Count only one medal per unique event and country so team sports are not overcounted
medals_unique <- olympics |>
  filter(!is.na(Medal)) |>
  distinct(Year, Season, Games, Sport, Event, NOC, Medal)

title: Olympic Comparisons by Sport
section: 1. Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. Selected European Countries
text:
1. Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. Selected European Countries

Which sports drive the overall medal totals between the United States and Europe? The interactive chart below shows the top 10 medal-winning sports across the USA and our 12 selected European countries from 1896 to 2016.
Even when compared against 12 European countries combined, the United States actually leads in Swimming (550 vs. 411) and is nearly tied in Athletics (816 vs. 822)! Meanwhile, the selected European nations have a large collective advantage in Fencing (424 vs. 32), Cycling (423 vs. 57), Canoeing (329 vs. 16), Rowing (314 vs. 89), and Cross Country Skiing (299 vs. 1).


Show R Code
# Find the top 10 sports overall by unique event medals among USA + 12 European countries
top_10_sports <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs)) |>
  count(Sport, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  pull(Sport)

# Count medals by Sport and Region for those top 10 sports
sports_comparison <- medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs), Sport %in% top_10_sports) |>
  mutate(
    Group = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(Sport, Group, name = "Medals") |>
  mutate(Sport = fct_reorder(Sport, Medals, .fun = sum))

# Build horizontal grouped bar chart
p_top_sports <- ggplot(sports_comparison, aes(x = Sport, y = Medals, fill = Group)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#ec4899",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Olympic Sports: USA vs. 12 European Countries (1896–2016)",
    subtitle = "Unique event medals won in the most contested Olympic sports",
    x = "Olympic Sport",
    y = "Unique Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_top_sports, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill")) |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

2. Spain’s Top 10 Medal-Winning Olympic Sports (1900–2016)

Focusing specifically on Spain (ESP), which sports have delivered the most Olympic success? Across Spain’s 150 unique event medals, water and endurance/racquet sports lead the way:

Sailing (19 medals: 13 Gold, 5 Silver, 1 Bronze) is Spain’s single most successful Olympic sport, accounting for more than a quarter of Spain’s 45 all-time Gold medals.
Canoeing (16 medals), Cycling (15 medals), Athletics (14 medals), and Tennis (12 medals) round out Spain’s top five sports.

title: Olympic Comparisons by Sport
section: 3. Athlete Age & Height Profiles by Sport (Connecting Physical Profiles to Sports)
text:
3. Athlete Age & Height Profiles by Sport (Connecting Physical Profiles to Sports)

On the Home page, we plotted 14,553 individual medal-winning athlete observations by age and height. Why do those points spread across such a wide range of ages and heights?
The interactive chart below compares the average age and average height of medalists in the 12 most common Olympic sports (separately for the United States and Selected Europe), where bubble size reflects the number of medalist observations:

Gymnastics (162–168 cm, ages 20–24) and Swimming (179–181 cm, ages 20–22) feature some of the youngest medalists.
Basketball (192–196 cm) and Rowing (185–186 cm) feature the tallest Olympic medalists.
Equestrianism (ages 34–38), Sailing (ages 29–32), and Shooting (ages 31–35) reward years of technical experience, producing the oldest average medalists.



Show R Code
# Compute sport-level average Age and Height across the top 12 sports by medalist count
top_12_medalist_sports <- olympics |>
  filter(NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs), !is.na(Medal), !is.na(Age), !is.na(Height)) |>
  count(Sport, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  pull(Sport)

sport_profiles <- olympics |>
  filter(
    NOC %in% c("USA", euro_nocs),
    !is.na(Medal),
    !is.na(Age),
    !is.na(Height),
    Sport %in% top_12_medalist_sports
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      NOC == "USA",
      "United States (USA)",
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(Sport, Region) |>
  summarise(
    Medalist_Count = n(),
    Mean_Age = round(mean(Age), 1),
    Mean_Height = round(mean(Height), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Hover_Text = paste0(
      "<b>", Sport, "</b><br>",
      "Region: ", Region, "<br>",
      "Average Age: <b>", Mean_Age, " yrs</b><br>",
      "Average Height: <b>", Mean_Height, " cm</b><br>",
      "Medalist Observations: ", format(Medalist_Count, big.mark = ",")
    )
  )

p_profiles <- ggplot(
  sport_profiles,
  aes(x = Mean_Age, y = Mean_Height, color = Region, size = Medalist_Count, text = Hover_Text)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Selected Europe (12 Countries)" = "#a855f7",
      "United States (USA)" = "#fbbf24"
    )
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(4, 13), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Age vs. Average Height Across 12 Major Olympic Sports",
    subtitle = "Bubble size indicates number of medalist observations; hover to inspect each sport",
    x = "Average Medalist Age (Years)",
    y = "Average Medalist Height (cm)",
    color = "Region / Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )

ggplotly(p_profiles, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    paper_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    plot_bgcolor = "#151c33",
    font = list(color = "#f8fafc"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.05, y = 1.12)
  )

title: Barcelona 1992: Spain’s Olympic Turning Point

text:
Spain Before, During, and After Barcelona 1992



Show R Code
# Fixed narrative chart comparing Spain's Summer Olympic medal totals across eras
ggplot(spain_summer_timeline, aes(x = Year, y = Total_Medals, fill = Era)) +
  # Shaded era background for the post-1992 era
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 1990, xmax = 2018, ymin = 0, ymax = 27.5,
    fill = "#a855f7", alpha = 0.08
  ) +
  # Pre-1992 average line (1.63 medals per Summer Games)
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 1898, xend = 1989.5, y = 26 / 16, yend = 26 / 16,
    color = "#cbd5e1", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.85
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1940, y = 4.3,
    label = "Pre-1992 Mean: 1.6 medals / Summer Games\n(26 total across 16 Summer Games)",
    color = "#cbd5e1", size = 3.4, fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  # Barcelona 1992 annotation placed in open space to the left with a pointer segment
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 1977, xend = 1990.3, y = 23.2, yend = 22.0,
    color = "#f472b6", linewidth = 0.75
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1956, y = 23.4,
    label = "Barcelona 1992: 22 Summer Medals (13 Gold)\n+ 1 Winter Bronze = 23 Total in 1992",
    color = "#f472b6", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  # Post-1992 average line (16.67 medals per Summer Games)
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = 1994.5, xend = 2017.5, y = 100 / 6, yend = 100 / 6,
    color = "#fbbf24", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.95
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2006, y = 25.3,
    label = "Post-1992 Mean: 16.7 medals / Games\n(100 total across 1996–2016)",
    color = "#fbbf24", size = 3.45, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  geom_col(width = 2.7, color = "#0b1021", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if_else(Total_Medals > 0, as.character(Total_Medals), "")),
    vjust = -0.45,
    color = "#f8fafc",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.35
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Before 1992 (1900–1988)" = "#64748b",
      "Barcelona 1992 (Host Year)" = "#ec4899",
      "After 1992 (1996–2016)" = "#a855f7"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2016, by = 8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 28), breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Spain's Summer Olympic Medal Totals Before, During, and After Barcelona 1992",
    subtitle = "Unique Summer Olympic event medals won by Spain (ESP) across all 23 Summer participations (1900–2016)",
    x = "Summer Olympic Year",
    y = "Unique Summer Event Medals Won",
    fill = "Olympic Era",
    caption = "Source: 120 Years of Olympic History (Kaggle). Counts deduplicated by unique event; Spain also won 2 Winter medals (1972 Gold, 1992 Bronze)."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#151c33", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#2a3558"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#fbbf24", face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1", size = 11.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#94a3b8", size = 9.5),
    text = element_text(color = "#f8fafc"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "#cbd5e1"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Figure 1





For nearly a century before 1992, Spain played a modest role in the Olympic Games. Counting unique event medals so that team sports are never overcounted, Spain won just 27 total medals across 92 years (1900–1988)—26 in the Summer Games (5 Gold, 12 Silver, and 9 Bronze across 16 Summer Olympic appearances) plus a single Winter Gold in 1972. Throughout that entire pre-1992 era, Spain averaged only 1.63 Summer medals per Games, went completely medal-less in multiple Summer appearances (1924, 1964, 1968), and never exceeded the 6 medals won at the boycotted 1980 Moscow Olympics.
A dramatic jump occurred when Barcelona hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics. In Barcelona 1992, Spain captured 22 unique Summer event medals (13 Gold, 7 Silver, 2 Bronze)—plus 1 Winter Bronze in Albertville for 23 total medals in 1992. In a single Summer Games on home soil, Spanish athletes won more than twice as many Gold medals (13) as Spain had won in its entire preceding Olympic history (6 total Golds from 1900 to 1988), led by Sailing (4 Gold, 1 Silver), Athletics (4 medals), Cycling (2 Gold), Judo (2 Gold), and team golds in Men’s Football and Women’s Field Hockey. Ahead of the Games, Spain had also introduced Plan ADO (Asociación Deportes Olímpicos) in 1988 to expand training centers, coaching, and athlete scholarships alongside host-country preparations.
Following 1992, Spain’s Olympic medal results remained substantially higher than in the pre-1992 era. Across the six Summer Olympic Games after Barcelona (1996–2016), Spain won 100 unique event medals (26 Gold, 44 Silver, 30 Bronze), averaging 16.7 medals per Summer Games—more than ten times its pre-1992 average (1.63)—and finishing between 11 and 20 medals at every Summer Games (82% of Spain’s 150 all-time medals were won in 1992 or later). While this timeline clearly shows that Spain’s Olympic results rose sharply in 1992 and stayed elevated afterward, the medal data alone is observational and cannot prove what caused that sustained improvement—which likely reflects a combination of long-term sports funding, new facilities, growing youth participation, broader economic growth in Spain, and the expansion of Olympic events over time.

title: Barcelona 1992: Spain’s Olympic Turning Point
section: Summary Table: Spain’s Olympic Medal Performance by Era (1900–2016)
text:
Summary Table: Spain’s Olympic Medal Performance by Era (1900–2016)

The table below compares Spain’s unique event medal totals across all three eras (showing both Summer-only totals and combined Summer + Winter totals):


Show R Code
medals_unique |>
  filter(NOC == "ESP") |>
  mutate(
    Era = case_when(
      Year < 1992 ~ "1. Before 1992 (1900–1988)",
      Year == 1992 ~ "2. Barcelona 1992 (Host Year)",
      Year > 1992 ~ "3. After 1992 (1996–2016)"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(Era) |>
  summarise(
    Summer_Games_Played = case_when(
      first(Era) == "1. Before 1992 (1900–1988)" ~ 16L,
      first(Era) == "2. Barcelona 1992 (Host Year)" ~ 1L,
      TRUE ~ 6L
    ),
    Total_Unique_Medals = n(),
    Summer_Medals = sum(Season == "Summer"),
    Winter_Medals = sum(Season == "Winter"),
    Gold = sum(Medal == "Gold"),
    Silver = sum(Medal == "Silver"),
    Bronze = sum(Medal == "Bronze"),
    Summer_Medals_Per_Games = round(sum(Season == "Summer") / first(Summer_Games_Played), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Olympic Era",
      "Summer Games Contested",
      "Total Unique Medals",
      "Summer Medals",
      "Winter Medals",
      "Gold",
      "Silver",
      "Bronze",
      "Summer Medals / Games"
    ),
    caption = "Spain's Unique Event Medal Performance Before, During, and After the 1992 Barcelona Games"
  )
